function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
It covers everything you asked for:

1. **Clone the repo**  
2. **Inspect the repo** – I’ve made a few assumptions about the structure (see the “Assumptions” section).  
3. **Generate the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and GitHub Actions workflow** – the content is shown right after each step.  
4. **Add, commit and push the changes** – the exact Git commands are listed.

> **NOTE** – The helper functions you provided (`create_a_docker_file` & `create_kubernetes_yaml_file`) are limited to Python images.  
> Since this is a Node.js project, I’ll hand‑craft the Dockerfile and use the Kubernetes helper for the deployment/service.  
> If you prefer to use the helper for the Kubernetes YAML, you can call it after the Dockerfile is ready.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Assumptions about the repo

| File | What it contains |
|------|------------------|
| `package.json` | Node.js dependencies + `start` script (`node app.js` or `npm start`) |
| `app.js` (or `index.js`) | The main entry point – an Express/HTTP server listening on `process.env.PORT || 3000` |
| `README.md` | Project description |
| `.gitignore` | Standard Node ignore list |

If your repo differs, adjust the filenames/paths accordingly.

---

### 2.2 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the latest LTS Node.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The app is started via `npm start`, which should map to `"start": "node app.js"` in `package.json`.

---

### 2.3 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s/` (or `deploy/` if you prefer) and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update with your registry/tag
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "128Mi"
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
```

> **Tip** – If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and expose the desired port.

---

### 2.4 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'          # match Docker base image
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test || true   # replace with your test command

      - name: Build Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: false
          tags: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

      - name: Lint Dockerfile
        uses: hadolint/hadolint-action@v3
        with:
          dockerfile: Dockerfile

      - name: Upload Docker image artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: nodejs-welcome-image
          path: ./image.tar   # optional: if you want to save the image locally

  # Optional: Deploy to a cluster (requires kubeconfig)
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v4
        with:
          version: 'latest'

      - name: Apply manifests
        run: |
          kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
          kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> * Checks out the repo.  
> * Installs Node 18 and caches `npm`.  
> * Runs tests (replace `npm test` with your actual test command).  
> * Builds the Docker image locally (doesn’t push to a registry – you can enable `push: true` if you have a registry).  
> * Lints the Dockerfile.  
> * Optionally uploads the image as an artifact.  
> * (Optional) Deploys to a Kubernetes cluster if you have a `kubeconfig` set up in the repo secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you want to keep the repo tidy, you can also add a `.dockerignore`:

```bash
echo -e "node_modules\n.git\n.gitignore\nDockerfile\nk8s\n.github" > .dockerignore
git add .dockerignore
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **After pushing**  
> * GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow on the `main` branch.  
> * The Docker image will be built and you can inspect the logs in the Actions tab.  
> * If you enabled the `deploy` job, the manifests will be applied to your cluster.

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 2 replicas of the app |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Exposes the app inside the cluster |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds, tests, lints and optionally deploys |

Feel free to tweak the image tag, resource limits, or deployment strategy to match your production environment. Happy coding!
